title: NBA Fines Clippers $30M, Strips Five Draft Picks, Bans Ballmer One Year for Salary-Cap Scheme
dek: The NBA concluded an investigation into the Clippers' salary-cap circumvention scheme involving player Kawhi Leonard. The league fined the team $30 million, stripped five first-round picks beginning in 2029, and banned owner Steve Ballmer from the league for one year. The Clippers said they vehemently reject the findings.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: The Clippers routed millions to Kawhi Leonard through third-party companies (Aspiration Partners, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics, and Lockton Insurance) in endorsement deals totaling $18 million, none of which were publicly announced, to circumvent salary-cap rules.
bottom_line: The Clippers have sworn to challenge the penalties through every available channel, setting up a protracted legal dispute over how far a franchise can go in fighting an NBA enforcement ruling. Whether the Clippers succeed in reducing or overturning the sanctions will define how effectively the league can police salary-cap circumvention by wealthy, sophisticated actors with legal resources to mount a sustained defense.
body: The NBA concluded a sweeping investigation into the Los Angeles Clippers' scheme to circumvent the league's salary-cap rules and handed down penalties that mark an uncommon enforcement action against a major franchise and its owner. Per Front Office Sports, the league fined the Clippers $30 million, stripped the team of five first-round picks starting in 2029, and banned owner Steve Ballmer from the league for one year. The penalties underscore what NBA Commissioner Adam Silver characterized as "flagrant violations" and "institutional and leadership failures."

The investigation, conducted by lawyers at Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and completed in 2026, found that the Clippers routed millions in off-the-books payments to player Kawhi Leonard through four third-party companies between 2020 and 2021. According to the report, Clippers executives coordinated endorsement deals with Aspiration Partners, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics, and Lockton Insurance. The three companies disclosed in prior reporting were Aspiration, Boingo, and Daktronics; Lockton's involvement had not been previously reported, per Front Office Sports.

The mechanism was deliberate. Clippers executive Zucker made email introductions connecting Leonard's agent Robertson to the companies over six days in early June 2020, framed in language "aimed at giving the appearance of complying with circumvention rules," according to the report. In July 2020, Leonard signed endorsement deals with two of the companies on the same day; within a month, he had signed a similar deal with the third. In total, those three agreements were worth $18 million, money paid to Leonard by August 2021. None of these agreements were publicly announced, defeating what the report described as "the foundational purpose of an endorsement agreement: to obtain associational benefits of the company's relationship with the endorser." All three companies also signed multimillion-dollar agreements with the Clippers, and investigators concluded the money the team paid to the companies "may in fact have been made principally to fund the endorsement deals with Mr. Leonard."

The investigation reviewed more than 200,000 pages of documents and interviewed 60 people, including Ballmer, team president Josh Zucker, chief legal officer Marcus Frank, Leonard, Robertson, Aspiration founder Joseph Sandberg, and representatives connected to the other companies. According to the report, Boingo initially said it would cooperate but supplied faulty information; Aspiration and Daktronics were helpful; Lockton refused to cooperate. The Clippers and their legal counsel "at times stifled the investigation by delaying their responses to requests for information and operating in an 'adversarial or obfuscatory manner that slowed investigators' ability to gather the facts.'"

Zucker made "several statements" inconsistent with documents and other witness testimony, claimed she could not remember details about "important issues," and blamed subordinates. Frank, by contrast, was "generally consistent across his interviews" and "took responsibility for the actions of subordinates." The report noted that "given the scope of this matter and its complexity" and "considering the public's interest," investigators continued to receive relevant information as of the report's completion.

The Clippers said late Wednesday that they "vehemently reject" the conclusions, calling the investigation "heavily biased," and said they plan to "vigorously challenge" the NBA sanctions "through every avenue available to us." Silver said: "The NBA's collectively bargained system for determining player compensation is a fundamental component of the basketball competition that the league oversees for the benefit of the teams and players and ultimately the fans. I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers' institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct. The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations." The league and union agreed to the punishments, and there will be no appeal, per Front Office Sports.
